question: What is different about how the sales team handles renewals versus new business?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every concrete action, statement, offer, or commitment that the OrbitFlow sales or account staff make during the call, including how they open the call, how they handle objections, pricing and discount offers, contract or term discussions, next steps, and any stated approach to the customer's goals, so that approaches in renewal calls can later be compared with approaches in new business (prospect) calls.
assumptions: 'Handles' is interpreted as the sales team's approach and tactics, not internal operations.
Renewal covers existing-customer calls (Renewal type); new business covers Prospect type calls.
Cold calls and churn post-mortems are excluded because the question contrasts renewals with new business only.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I actually spent three years at a freight forwarder before I moved into software.
findings.context: OrbitFlow AE opened the call by building rapport through shared background (former freight forwarder middle-office experience) before turning to discovery. — New business discovery/first demo call; opener is rapport-building, not renewal-specific.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Not the full tour. I'd rather skip the bits that aren't relevant.
findings.context: OrbitFlow AE framed the call approach as understanding the customer's current process first, then showing only relevant product parts rather than a full tour. — Discovery-led approach in a new business call; customer had previously sat through full tours from three vendors.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month, that's up to thirty users, annual agreement. Enterprise is custom — that's where the governance and security capabilities sit, plus higher usage.
findings.context: When the customer asked for pricing early, OrbitFlow disclosed list-level tiers (Growth from $1,800/month up to 30 users on annual agreement; Enterprise custom) without a quote. — Pricing disclosure in response to customer asking 'what does this cost' before the deeper discovery; customer said the number was higher than expected and anchored on Zapier.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: It's a very common anchor. It's also the wrong one, but I'd rather earn that than assert it.
findings.context: OrbitFlow AE handled the price objection by saying the Zapier price anchor is common and wrong, but preferred to demonstrate value rather than assert it. — Objection handling on pricing; customer said they had benchmarked against Zapier, which they acknowledged was not a fair comparison.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Let's come back to that properly later — I don't want to give you a number before I know your user model, because that's exactly where proposals become misleading.
findings.context: OrbitFlow AE deferred a firm pricing number until the user model was understood, explicitly declining to give a number on the call. — Pricing deferral in a new business deal; the stated reason is that early numbers could mislead the proposal.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'm deliberately not giving you an exact number today because without the user model any number I give you is misleading.
findings.context: OrbitFlow AE again declined to quote an exact number on user licensing and committed to an itemised proposal covering builders, viewers/approvers, workflow volume, and one-time services. — Pricing and licensing discussion; customer asked that per-user approver costs be explicit to avoid surprises later.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: It'll be itemised — assumed builder count, viewer and approver population, expected workflow volume, and any one-time services separately.
findings.context: OrbitFlow committed to an itemised proposal separating assumed builder count, viewer/approver population, expected workflow volume, and one-time services. — Commitment on proposal structure in response to customer request for transparency about per-seat costs.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Noted, and agreed — that belongs in the contract, not on a call.
findings.context: OrbitFlow AE agreed to put the customer's data-use commitment into the contract rather than rely on a verbal statement on the call. — Contract/terms discussion; the vendor's staff member agreed the no-training-on-customer-data promise belongs in the contract.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: And a perfectly valid outcome is "don't buy OrbitFlow" if the existing approach meets the criteria more cheaply.
findings.context: OrbitFlow AE stated that not buying OrbitFlow is a valid outcome if the status quo meets criteria more cheaply, and proposed defining the pilot against status quo and alternatives. — Stated approach to the customer's goals in a new business evaluation; customer compared against Workato and improving existing tools.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: we send the security pack and a short architecture summary, you send the representative workflow and sample data, and we jointly write three to five pilot success criteria.
findings.context: OrbitFlow AE set out next steps: vendor sends security pack and architecture summary; customer supplies a representative workflow and sample data; both jointly write pilot success criteria before a sandbox decision. — Next-steps close of a new business call; no renewal-specific steps discussed.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: We'll write it up as a pilot exit criterion. If we can't satisfy it, that should be an explicit result, not something that surfaces in procurement at the end.
findings.context: OrbitFlow AE committed to treating a customer-raised commercial gate (expansion of existing Workato contract) as an explicit pilot exit criterion. — Objection/gate handling; the customer said the internal commercial question of Workato expansion is their main hurdle.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: If security's a no, the rest is theatre.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's AE opened the call by putting security first and framing it as the gate for everything else. — New-business prospect call (not a renewal). Opening approach: agreed to the customer's security-first request.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'm not going to give you a yes on this call.
findings.context: The AE refused to give a yes on the BAA during the call and committed only to a written position within a week. — Objection handling on a regulatory gate; avoided a verbal commitment.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month for up to thirty users on an annual agreement. Enterprise is custom-priced
findings.context: The AE set out Growth pricing as a headline figure and positioned the prospect for Enterprise, not Growth, based on its requirements. — Pricing and package discussion; Growth is annual, Enterprise custom-priced.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: let me build the model around your actual user population rather than a headline number.
findings.context: The AE declined to quote a price until the user model was known, and proposed building the model around the actual user population. — Pricing approach: withheld a figure rather than give a headline number.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: It'll be itemised. Assumed builders, viewer and approver population, expected workflow volume, one-time services separately.
findings.context: The AE said the proposal would be itemised by user role and volume, with one-time services separate. — Proposal structure commitment in response to customer request for clarity on seat types.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Procurement will not have a serious pricing conversation until security tells us whether the BAA requirement can be met.
findings.context: The customer said procurement would not discuss pricing until security answered the BAA question, so the AE's pricing discussion was on hold. — Customer's stated sequencing for commercial talks; price not yet discussed.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: we won't try to replace everything. Plenty of customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep integration
findings.context: The AE positioned OrbitFlow as complementary to existing iPaaS and Microsoft tooling rather than a full replacement, and said a migrate-everything pitch would lose to the customer's licensing. — Approach to the incumbent Power Automate and Microsoft agreement; competitive positioning.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: a valid outcome is
findings.context: The AE said that a pilot should be measured against the status quo and Power Automate, and that 'don't buy' is a valid outcome. — Closing approach to the evaluation; openly allowed a no-purchase result.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: For a pilot we can baseline one or two things before automating.
findings.context: The AE proposed a pilot-stage baseline (elapsed time, manual touches, exception rate, systems-group hours) before automating. — ROI approach for the pilot rather than a headcount-based business case.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Concrete next steps then.
findings.context: The AE set out concrete next steps: send security pack, written BAA position within a week, customer sends a representative workflow, and joint pilot success criteria. — Closing next-steps commitment.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: So normally I'd spend twenty minutes on discovery before showing anything, but —
findings.context: Call is a new-business prospect call (discovery/demo), not a renewal; no renewal or existing-contract discussion occurred. — Call type is Prospect; Leo opens by proposing discovery and then demo.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Deal. I'll ask about four questions along the way rather than up front. Fair?
findings.context: Vendor opened by planning a standard discovery-then-demo approach, but adapted to the prospect's request to skip discovery and go straight to a demo, with four questions asked along the way. — Prospect pushed back on discovery; Leo agreed to adapt.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I'll come back with what they'd look like rebuilt here
findings.context: Vendor declined to make up technical answers and committed to written follow-up from a solutions engineer. — Solutions engineer unavailable on the call; technical questions deferred.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: It's a meaningful discount, not a transformation.
findings.context: On price, vendor acknowledged the gap between the Growth list price and the prospect's budget and did not pretend otherwise; offered annual prepay as a discount but said it is not a large reduction. — Objection handling on pricing for a prospect whose budget was about half the quoted price.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month, up to thirty users, on an annual agreement.
findings.context: Vendor stated Growth pricing as starting at £1,800 a month for up to 30 users on an annual agreement, and EU data residency is only on Enterprise. — Contract/term and tier details presented to a prospect.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: But you could count it for four weeks before you decide anything. That's free and it'd make the conversation much easier either way.
findings.context: Vendor prompted the prospect to quantify the cost of the current setup and proposed a free four-week measurement exercise before deciding. — Value-building approach tied to prospect's internal business case.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Then let me put the assumptions in writing and you can hold me to them.
findings.context: Vendor said usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connectors and committed to modelling costs in writing rather than saying no. — Prospect asked about extra costs for AI features.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Understood. That's useful to know now rather than in six weeks.
findings.context: Vendor asked about the buyer's approval path and timing, learning that spend above £15k/year goes to COO and finance director; vendor noted this early. — Decision-making process and timeline discovery.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Big-bang migrations of sixty automations is how these projects die.
findings.context: Vendor's stated next steps: written answers on Shopify trigger coverage and processing region, and a rebuild of the prospect's three worst automations with an honest comparison, with a suggestion to migrate incrementally. — Agreed next steps at close of call.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: It might be. I'd rather you concluded that in July than in month five.
findings.context: Vendor framed the competitive bar honestly as beating Zapier plus better documentation, not beating doing nothing, and said the prospect might conclude to stay put. — Competitive and objection framing for a new-business prospect.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
findings.context: Prospect's stated reason for hesitation is value versus price against existing tools, not a renewal issue; prospect said they are not saying no. — Prospect's closing position on the call.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I'd rather have a considered maybe than an enthusiastic yes that dies in procurement.
findings.context: Vendor's sales approach emphasised a considered maybe over pressure, and said a qualified decision is preferable to an enthusiastic yes that dies in procurement. — Closing stance with a budget-constrained prospect.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I sent an agenda but I'd rather you told me if it's wrong.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's AE opened the call by asking for agenda corrections and deferred the demo at the customer's request, treating the prospect's stated priorities as the agenda. — New-business prospect discovery call, not a renewal. Customer asked to drop the product demo and focus on architecture and governance.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: For the record — Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement, but that's not your shape. You're an Enterprise conversation. Custom priced, advanced governance, security capabilities, higher usage.
findings.context: On pricing, OrbitFlow stated Growth-tier list pricing to the prospect, positioned it as not applicable, and moved the account to a custom-priced Enterprise conversation. — New-business pricing discussion. Growth tier is a published list price; Enterprise is custom priced. No discount or renewal terms were offered.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Then here's what I'll commit to. The proposal will separate licence, assumed builder count, viewer and approver population, expected workflow volume, and services as distinct line items, with the assumptions written next to each.
findings.context: OrbitFlow committed to transparent proposal pricing, splitting licence, builder count, viewer/approver population, workflow volume and services into separate line items, and marking unknowns as to-be-determined rather than placeholder numbers. — Response to the customer's concern about surprise costs in professional services, premium connectors and post-architecture discovery.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: If phase one requires significant SAP and on-premise work, that's professional services, and I'd rather price it honestly up front than have it appear after architecture review.
findings.context: OrbitFlow proactively flagged that phase-one SAP and on-prem work would be professional services and said it would price that up front. — Commercial disclosure raised by the vendor before the customer asked about it.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'm not going to give you a number today because without the user model any number is misleading.
findings.context: OrbitFlow declined to give a per-seat or licence number before the user model was defined, citing that any number would be misleading. — Customer asked what counts as a user and whether occasional approvers need full seats.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: It's slow, but it's honest, and a slow honest timeline is worth more to me than a fast invented one.
findings.context: OrbitFlow framed the timeline honestly rather than promising a fast close, citing past missed Q3 dates. — Vendor response to customer's slow procurement and architecture timeline (September review, Q4 procurement, early next year production).

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: That's a strategically sound position and I'm not going to argue with it.
findings.context: OrbitFlow accepted the customer's position to defer generative AI from phase one and did not push back. — Objection handling: customer wanted no GenAI in phase one due to review burden. Vendor agreed rather than arguing, and noted AI steps are optional.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: And the next step is architecture material, not a sandbox.
findings.context: OrbitFlow closed with a summary and set the next step as architecture material and deferred sandbox/pilot, agreeing to the customer's gated path rather than pushing a trial. — Next-step handling in a new-business prospect call. Customer explicitly rejected a sandbox as premature; vendor accepted and committed to a written recap with open questions separated from confirmed requirements.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's Growth tier is quoted at $1,800 a month for up to 30 users on an annual agreement, and this prospect is not a Growth fit, so it is steered to custom-priced Enterprise. — New-business pricing discussion on a prospect call; the prospect has ~40 builders and up to 300 approvers/viewers, so tier fit was assessed against seat count.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: it's exactly why I won't quote you a number before I know it.
findings.context: OrbitFlow will not quote a price until seat counts are known, and will itemise licensed builders versus approval-only or notification-only users in the proposal. — Prospect asked what counts as a user; the vendor deferred a number and committed to a split in writing.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: agree what happens above the threshold before you sign, and put the overage mechanism in the contract explicitly rather than in a rate card that changes.
findings.context: Usage overage will be handled by modelling the prospect's expected volumes, agreeing the above-threshold terms before signing, and writing the overage mechanism explicitly into the contract rather than a changeable rate card. — Prospect (Noah Williams) raised concern about second-year invoice surprises from usage overages seen with other vendors.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I don't want to promise a specific structure on a call before I've modelled your volumes
findings.context: OrbitFlow declined to promise a usage cap on the call, deliberately avoiding an unconditional yes before volumes are modelled. — Prospect asked 'Can you cap it?'; vendor said mechanisms exist but would not commit to a structure.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Then I'll model three hundred and five hundred and you can see the shape of the curve rather than a point estimate.
findings.context: OrbitFlow will model pricing at 300 and 500 users to show the cost curve rather than a single point estimate, and asked the prospect for volume estimates to do so. — Commercial next step; prospect's volume estimates were due the following Friday, and the prospect asked for the overage modelling to run in parallel with the pilot.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: It needs to be contractual for you to rely on it, and I'd expect legal to insist.
findings.context: Contract language is the vendor's position for any data-use commitment; OrbitFlow acknowledged the customer's legal team would require it to be contractual. — Prospect asked whether the 'no training on customer data' commitment was contractual or marketing.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: a six-week pilot proposal with three to five success criteria that we write jointly, not that I write and you approve.
findings.context: OrbitFlow proposed a six-week paid pilot with three to five success criteria to be written jointly with the customer, and a documented workflow design standard that the customer keeps regardless of purchase. — Pilot framing offered in response to the customer's request to compare against Tray.io; the sales lead used the pilot as the path to a purchase decision.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Then let's say the pack goes out tomorrow, sandbox by end of next week, pilot starts the week after.
findings.context: OrbitFlow set a timeline for the pack, sandbox, and pilot start, and said the deliverable of a documented design standard is kept whether or not the customer buys. — Next steps agreed on the call; the prospect's technical bake-off and vendor decision dates were fixed by a remediation programme.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I'd rather we lose to a documented decision than lose to a two-month detour.
findings.context: When the customer raised the 'keep scripts and document them' option, the vendor chose to address it openly in the pilot criteria rather than position Tray as the only alternative, and said it would rather lose to a documented decision than to a long internal detour. — Competitive and status-quo objection handling on a prospect call; the customer confirmed it would not satisfy the auditor.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Hannah, can you define what you mean by model risk in your context?
findings.context: OrbitFlow's sales approach on this prospect call was to ask clarifying questions about the buyer's terms before answering, and to avoid overstating capabilities (e.g., declining to call the AI-output limitation a switch or claiming unit-test equivalence). — Technical and governance objection handling, which the vendor linked to the buyer's need to avoid over-claim; this is a new-business prospect call, not a renewal.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: agencies are honestly our sweet spot at the moment
findings.context: Alastair opened by framing the call around OrbitFlow's agency track record and a general product pitch before asking about the prospect's pain. — New business discovery opening; sets the approach used with prospects rather than renewals.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: our Growth package is eighteen hundred a month, up to thirty users, on an annual agreement
findings.context: Alastair told the prospect that the Growth package is 1,800 a month for up to thirty users on an annual agreement. — Pricing offered during new business discovery; annual term is the default.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: Yeah, monthly's usually fine, we can sort something out.
findings.context: When asked for ten users or monthly billing, Alastair first said monthly was usually fine, then said he would need to check with his manager; he also said the thirty-user package price is fixed. — Negotiation on term and seat count in a prospect call; the answer was not confirmed on the call.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: The thirty is the package, so the price is the price.
findings.context: Alastair said the thirty-user package price is fixed, so the price is the price, and pointed to room to grow rather than offering fewer seats. — Response to a request to pay for fewer seats; no discount offered.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: mate, what's a lost client worth?
findings.context: When the prospect said the price was above budget and above her spending limit, Alastair answered with an ROI-style story about a past deal and a lost-client framing rather than a discount or concession. — Objection handling on price in a new business call; the prospect's founder approval threshold was raised.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: I moved off that account so I'm not across the detail. But they renewed, I think.
findings.context: Alastair said he moved off the referenced account and was not sure whether it renewed, then offered to find a reference. — Customer asked whether the earlier deal solved the problem; the renewal evidence is uncertain.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: Yeah, I can do a Loom.
findings.context: Alastair committed to a recorded, tailored demo by end of week and to sending a DPA and reference, and to confirming monthly billing and SSO terms. — Next steps set at the end of a new business call.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: you'd be back here in eighteen months.
findings.context: Prospect said the ops-driven decision would go to the founder and that Zapier plus process discipline is a real alternative; Alastair responded that they would be back in eighteen months. — Competitive and value pushback in new business; the prospect said they were interested but not dismissing alternatives.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: Yeah, all plans.
findings.context: Alastair said OrbitFlow's SSO is included on all plans, which the customer questioned and Alastair said he was fairly sure of but would confirm. — Feature/plan claim made to a prospect; customer said competitors gate it to enterprise.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement. Enterprise is custom priced
findings.context: OrbitFlow's sales lead stated list pricing for the Growth tier and that Enterprise is custom priced, on an annual agreement. — New-business discovery call; pricing given early and framed by tier, with no discount offered.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'm deliberately not giving you a number today, because without knowing your builder count versus your approver count any number I give you would be misleading in one direction or the other.
findings.context: The AE declined to give a per-seat number, saying a figure without knowing builder versus approver counts would mislead, and asked for the licensing shape to be explicit in writing. — Customer raised licensing model concern about hundreds of approvers; vendor deferred quoting a number.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'm not going to pretend we can beat bundled licensing on price. If the decision is purely cost per seat, Microsoft wins and everyone knows it.
findings.context: On the Power Automate price objection, the AE conceded OrbitFlow cannot beat bundled licensing on price and reframed the case around operational cost. — Objection handling for an incumbent bundled-licence comparison.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Do the same test in Power Automate at the same time. If it's not better, you should know.
findings.context: The AE proposed benchmarking OrbitFlow against the incumbent Power Automate and suggested the customer measure current debugging time for free, rather than pushing for a close. — Evaluation-stage approach; vendor encouraged a fair test even though it risked losing.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: A slow honest deal is worth more than a fast imaginary one.
findings.context: The AE stated a preference for an honest, slower deal over a fast forecast, and accepted that no decision would happen this year. — Customer said realistically no decision this year, budgeting starts October; vendor accepted timing rather than pushing.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: And from us in writing — the UK residency answer, and a note on the regional workspace and permissions design.
findings.context: The AE committed to next steps in writing (UK residency answer, regional workspace and permissions note) and an architecture and roadmap session, with the solutions engineer declining to commit to roadmap dates. — Closing next steps for a new-prospect evaluation; the offer was an architecture session, not a commercial proposal, because the customer asked for that.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: I'd rather have a roadmap and architecture conversation than a commercial proposal at this point.
findings.context: The customer said they wanted a roadmap and architecture conversation rather than a commercial proposal at this stage, so the vendor's next step was technical rather than commercial. — Customer-stated preference shaping the sales approach; no renewal or existing-contract discussion occurred on this call.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement. You're not a Growth shape — everything Samir's asked for sits in Enterprise, which is custom priced.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's sales lead quoted new-business pricing for a prospect: Growth at 1,800 per month up to 30 users on an annual agreement, with the required features placed in custom-priced Enterprise. — New-business pricing discussion on a prospect call; no renewal or existing-contract pricing is discussed.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Then the proposal should be scoped to the low-risk operational tier explicitly, with the privileged-content question marked as out of scope rather than as a future upsell.
findings.context: The sales lead committed to scoping the proposal to the low-risk operational tier, with privileged-content use marked out of scope rather than offered as a future upsell. — Response to the customer saying they would not make a business case that assumes privileged client content use; a scope-and-no-upsell commitment.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I'm not giving you a number today because without the split it'd be misleading.
findings.context: The sales lead declined to give a seat-based price, saying a number without the licence split would mislead. — Pricing objection/question from the customer about what counts as a user; the vendor deferred a number rather than quoting one.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: where we don't know, it'll say so rather than showing a placeholder that looks like a quote.
findings.context: The sales lead committed to separating professional services as its own line item with written assumptions, and to stating unknowns rather than showing placeholder figures that look like a quote. — Handling of implementation cost, which the vendor expects to be significant because of iManage and Intapp integration work.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: If the effort exceeds the value, you shouldn't do it, and I'd rather you concluded that in September than next March.
findings.context: The sales lead proposed testing the value case before buying, and said he would rather the customer reject the purchase early than late. — Handling of the customer's objection that integration effort may be disproportionate to value; the vendor offered a go/no-go test rather than arguing for the sale.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I won't dress a roadmap item as a capability.
findings.context: The sales lead refused to present a roadmap item as an existing capability, and declined to answer a compliance question (UK data residency) on the call, committing instead to a written answer. — Customer asked for firm yes/no answers rather than roadmap promises; vendor separated confirmed capability from roadmap and deferred the answer to writing.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: I'll get you a definitive answer within the week.
findings.context: The solutions engineer declined to answer the UK residency question on the call and committed to a definitive written answer within a week. — Customer pressed on UK residency, which may be a gate for public-sector clients; the vendor refused a verbal yes.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Then that maintenance burden is a real cost and it should be in the business case, not discovered later.
findings.context: The sales lead said the ongoing maintenance burden of a feature should be included in the business case rather than discovered later, and recommended documenting a limitation as deferred rather than solved. — Customer described barrier changes that occur weekly; the vendor advised costing the maintenance up front and documenting the gap.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: That's fine and I'd rather have it than an optimistic date.
findings.context: The sales lead set out next steps: send a security pack and written answers, receive the customer's operations list, and then return with an integration assessment and services estimate, with a Q4 proof of concept and Q1 decision. — Closing next-steps and timeline discussion for a new-business prospect; the vendor stated a timeline based on the customer's realistic schedule rather than an optimistic date.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Olivia, I know you've got a hard stop at half past so I'll keep us moving.
findings.context: Maya Chen opened the call by setting a time constraint and then stating the agenda, starting with the use case so both sides were solving the same problem. — Opening approach in a prospect (new business) call. Not a renewal call; there is no renewal-specific opening in this transcript.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'd suggest making it the first thing, honestly. It's the cheapest way to find out whether this project should exist.
findings.context: Maya Chen framed the value of the design and the pilot as cheap, early validation: test the signal against history before buying, rather than discovering a gap in a pilot. — Handling of a skeptical buyer. OrbitFlow's own SE (Jon Bell) made the same backward-test suggestion, and the customer's CS leader was surprised by it.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I won't quote a figure today because without that split any figure I give would mislead you in one direction or the other.
findings.context: Maya Chen stated that OrbitFlow would not quote a price until the user split (builders versus task recipients) was defined, and promised an itemised proposal with assumptions. — Pricing discussion in a prospect call. Pricing was given as list tiers only, with no discount or negotiated figure offered.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement.
findings.context: Maya Chen quoted list pricing: Growth at a fixed monthly rate up to thirty users on an annual agreement, with Enterprise custom-priced. — Contract term was framed as annual. No discount was offered; Enterprise pricing was deferred.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Then say it. I'd rather lose that way.
findings.context: Maya Chen chose to surface the competitor (expanding Gainsight) directly and build a cost comparison that includes it, and said she would rather lose than hide the spend question. — Competitive objection handling. The customer's existing spend on Gainsight was described as questionable, so the comparison may favour the incumbent.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Whether earlier intervention improves renewal is a separate hypothesis

findings.speaker: Leo Grant

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I'm not going to auto-renew you into a twelve-month contract you didn't intend to sign.

findings.quote: It's not a product feature you can buy, it's how our team allocates time, and I don't want to dress that up as something it isn't.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I'll write it accurately. You can decide whether it's compelling.
findings.context: The vendor said it would send the six-month proposal and a one-page comparison of renew versus lapse, written accurately including what the customer would lose. — Next step for finance; vendor offered the case for lapsing too.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: Regardless of what you decide. You should have that anyway and it shouldn't be a leaving-related request.
findings.context: The vendor committed to providing the data export of workflow definitions and run data regardless of the renewal decision, not as a leaving-related request. — Customer-favourable data portability commitment in renewal.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi

findings.context: The renewal price change is a seven percent standard uplift, presented as the only change to the contract. — Pricing discussion in a renewal; the customer accepted it without negotiation ('That's fine').

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: AI usage sits within your run allocation but there's a consumption element.
findings.context: The AI feature has a consumption-based cost element on top of the run allocation, which the vendor said would be quantified in the renewal papers and was not expected to change the renewal. — Commercial add-on surfaced during the renewal, proactively flagged by the vendor so the customer would not be surprised.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: I'll put a number on it so nobody's surprised, but I don't think it changes your renewal.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: It's thirty days for your contract. I checked before the call because I assumed you'd ask.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: I'd rather point that out than have your own auditor point it out.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: Renewal is agreed subject to papers — seven percent, no other changes, AI consumption estimate included.
findings.context: The renewal was summarised as agreed subject to papers at seven percent with no other changes, and the vendor committed to delivering the renewal papers by Wednesday. — Next steps and closing of a renewal call; the customer confirmed the summary as accurate.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: It's the only reason I get invited back.
findings.context: The vendor's CSM said the account management attention is what earns continued invitations, and asked the customer what had worked best over eighteen months. — Relationship framing at the end of a renewal call; a retention-oriented stance rather than a new-business pitch.

draft.answer: Renewal calls were run by account staff (CSM Ruth Adeyemi, AE Maya Chen or Leo Grant) in a retention-oriented way: they opened with account facts, cited a standard 7% uplift, right-sized seats, and gave concessions or exit options [C1][C2][C3]. In prospect calls the AEs ran discovery or demos, quoted the $1,800/month Growth list tier and steered larger prospects to custom Enterprise, withheld firm numbers until the user model was known, and set up pilots or evaluations [C4][C5][C6]. Both sides stressed candour, but in renewals it showed up as proactive disclosure and customer-favourable terms [C7][C8].

claims.text: Renewal calls opened with account facts and candour rather than a pitch: Lumen's call merged the QBR and renewal (Ruth Adeyemi), Halberd's opened with a one-sentence renewal summary, and Pinewood's opened with the 29 November renewal date and a ~40% usage drop.

Renewal pricing was formulaic and favoured the customer. A 7% standard uplift applied to everyone (Lumen, Maya Chen, not negotiable in principle; Halberd, accepted without negotiation). At Lumen the seats were cut from nine to seven with a higher run tier (400k), and the vendor said it was not inflating the tier to compensate. The vendor recommended a two-year term, declined to guess a multi-year discount without modelling, and promised a proposal by Friday with last year's and next year's line items side by side.

At-risk Pinewood renewal: Leo Grant withdrew his own Growth suggestion because SAML SSO is Enterprise-only, offered non-renewal or a six-month term at the pro-rata annual rate with no uplift, no auto-renew and free enablement, disclosed the 30 September notice deadline, offered a renew-versus-lapse comparison and a data export regardless of the decision, and CSM Ruth Adeyemi proposed a remediation plan. The customer said this candour increased their trust.

Prospect calls were run by AEs (Maya Chen, Leo Grant, Alastair McCrae) around discovery, a tailored demo or an evaluation, and often quoted Growth list pricing ($1,800/month up to 30 users, annual), steering several prospects (DeltaWorks, Ember, Harbor Legal, Juniper, BrightPath) to custom-priced Enterprise.

Prospect pricing was deferred until the user model was known, with itemised proposals promised (Acme, BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Ember, Greenline, Harbor Legal, Inkwell, Juniper). Alastair McCrae at Fable Media was the exception: he held the price as fixed, said monthly billing was 'usually fine' before saying he'd check with his manager, and answered the budget objection with a lost-client ROI story.

Prospect deals were moved forward through pilots or evaluations with jointly written success criteria, such as Ember's six-week pilot and Juniper's four-week evaluation, and the vendor openly allowed a 'don't buy' outcome (Acme, BrightPath, Cedar & Finch) or accepted slow timelines (DeltaWorks, Greenline).

Prospect-call candour took the form of honesty about competitors and price: Greenline was told Microsoft wins on pure per-seat cost, and Ember's vendor said it would rather lose to a documented decision. Written follow-ups replaced verbal commitments on compliance, for example the written UK residency answer for Harbor Legal.

Renewal candour was proactive disclosure of things the vendor might have kept quiet: overage waivers at Lumen, the AI consumption cost and the governance gap at Halberd, and the notice deadline at Pinewood.

not_covered: No renewal-specific data on win/loss or outcomes beyond what was said on the calls (Lumen's customer was to return the week of the 15th; Halberd was agreed subject to papers).
Only three renewal calls were read, so differences from new business reflect a small sample.
assumptions: 'Handles' means the sales approach and tactics, not internal operations.
Renewal means Renewal-type calls; new business means Prospect-type calls.
Cold calls and churn post-mortems are excluded.

evidence.context: OrbitFlow AE framed the call approach as understanding the customer's current process first, then showing only relevant product parts rather than a full tour. — Discovery-led approach in a new business call; customer had previously sat through full tours from three vendors.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month, that's up to thirty users, annual agreement. Enterprise is custom — that's where the governance and security capabilities sit, plus higher usage.
evidence.context: When the customer asked for pricing early, OrbitFlow disclosed list-level tiers (Growth from $1,800/month up to 30 users on annual agreement; Enterprise custom) without a quote. — Pricing disclosure in response to customer asking 'what does this cost' before the deeper discovery; customer said the number was higher than expected and anchored on Zapier.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: For the record — Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement, but that's not your shape. You're an Enterprise conversation. Custom priced, advanced governance, security capabilities, higher usage.
evidence.context: On pricing, OrbitFlow stated Growth-tier list pricing to the prospect, positioned it as not applicable, and moved the account to a custom-priced Enterprise conversation. — New-business pricing discussion. Growth tier is a published list price; Enterprise is custom priced. No discount or renewal terms were offered.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow's Growth tier is quoted at $1,800 a month for up to 30 users on an annual agreement, and this prospect is not a Growth fit, so it is steered to custom-priced Enterprise. — New-business pricing discussion on a prospect call; the prospect has ~40 builders and up to 300 approvers/viewers, so tier fit was assessed against seat count.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement. You're not a Growth shape — everything Samir's asked for sits in Enterprise, which is custom priced.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow's sales lead quoted new-business pricing for a prospect: Growth at 1,800 per month up to 30 users on an annual agreement, with the required features placed in custom-priced Enterprise. — New-business pricing discussion on a prospect call; no renewal or existing-contract pricing is discussed.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users, annual. You're an Enterprise conversation given the security list.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow AE Leo Grant gave pricing indication up front and called the account an Enterprise conversation given security requirements. — New-business pricing approach: quoting a tier price during evaluation rather than in a renewal context.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month for up to thirty users on an annual agreement. Enterprise is custom-priced
evidence.context: The AE set out Growth pricing as a headline figure and positioned the prospect for Enterprise, not Growth, based on its requirements. — Pricing and package discussion; Growth is annual, Enterprise custom-priced.

claims.text: Prospect pricing was deferred until the user model was known, with itemised proposals promised (Acme, BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Ember, Greenline, Harbor Legal, Inkwell, Juniper). Alastair McCrae at Fable Media was the exception: he held the price as fixed, said monthly billing was 'usually fine' before saying he'd check with his manager, and answered the budget objection with a lost-client ROI story.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Let's come back to that properly later — I don't want to give you a number before I know your user model, because that's exactly where proposals become misleading.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow AE deferred a firm pricing number until the user model was understood, explicitly declining to give a number on the call. — Pricing deferral in a new business deal; the stated reason is that early numbers could mislead the proposal.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: let me build the model around your actual user population rather than a headline number.
evidence.context: The AE declined to quote a price until the user model was known, and proposed building the model around the actual user population. — Pricing approach: withheld a figure rather than give a headline number.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: It'll be itemised. Assumed builders, viewer and approver population, expected workflow volume, one-time services separately.
evidence.context: The AE said the proposal would be itemised by user role and volume, with one-time services separate. — Proposal structure commitment in response to customer request for clarity on seat types.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: I'm not going to give you a number today because without the user model any number is misleading.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow declined to give a per-seat or licence number before the user model was defined, citing that any number would be misleading. — Customer asked what counts as a user and whether occasional approvers need full seats.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: it's exactly why I won't quote you a number before I know it.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow will not quote a price until seat counts are known, and will itemise licensed builders versus approval-only or notification-only users in the proposal. — Prospect asked what counts as a user; the vendor deferred a number and committed to a split in writing.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: I'm deliberately not giving you a number today, because without knowing your builder count versus your approver count any number I give you would be misleading in one direction or the other.
evidence.context: The AE declined to give a per-seat number, saying a figure without knowing builder versus approver counts would mislead, and asked for the licensing shape to be explicit in writing. — Customer raised licensing model concern about hundreds of approvers; vendor deferred quoting a number.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: I'm not giving you a number today because without the split it'd be misleading.
evidence.context: The sales lead declined to give a seat-based price, saying a number without the licence split would mislead. — Pricing objection/question from the customer about what counts as a user; the vendor deferred a number rather than quoting one.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: I won't quote a figure today because without that split any figure I give would mislead you in one direction or the other.
evidence.context: Maya Chen stated that OrbitFlow would not quote a price until the user split (builders versus task recipients) was defined, and promised an itemised proposal with assumptions. — Pricing discussion in a prospect call. Pricing was given as list tiers only, with no discount or negotiated figure offered.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: You'll have it in week two. I'll need volume estimates from you
evidence.context: Leo Grant committed to delivering the pricing model in writing before the evaluation ends, in week two. — Customer asked for economics early; sales committed to a written pricing model and asked for volume estimates first.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: Yeah, monthly's usually fine, we can sort something out.
evidence.context: When asked for ten users or monthly billing, Alastair first said monthly was usually fine, then said he would need to check with his manager; he also said the thirty-user package price is fixed. — Negotiation on term and seat count in a prospect call; the answer was not confirmed on the call.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: The thirty is the package, so the price is the price.
evidence.context: Alastair said the thirty-user package price is fixed, so the price is the price, and pointed to room to grow rather than offering fewer seats. — Response to a request to pay for fewer seats; no discount offered.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: mate, what's a lost client worth?
evidence.context: When the prospect said the price was above budget and above her spending limit, Alastair answered with an ROI-style story about a past deal and a lost-client framing rather than a discount or concession. — Objection handling on price in a new business call; the prospect's founder approval threshold was raised.

claims.text: Prospect deals were moved forward through pilots or evaluations with jointly written success criteria, such as Ember's six-week pilot and Juniper's four-week evaluation, and the vendor openly allowed a 'don't buy' outcome (Acme, BrightPath, Cedar & Finch) or accepted slow timelines (DeltaWorks, Greenline).

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: we send the security pack and a short architecture summary, you send the representative workflow and sample data, and we jointly write three to five pilot success criteria.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow AE set out next steps: vendor sends security pack and architecture summary; customer supplies a representative workflow and sample data; both jointly write pilot success criteria before a sandbox decision. — Next-steps close of a new business call; no renewal-specific steps discussed.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: a six-week pilot proposal with three to five success criteria that we write jointly, not that I write and you approve.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow proposed a six-week paid pilot with three to five success criteria to be written jointly with the customer, and a documented workflow design standard that the customer keeps regardless of purchase. — Pilot framing offered in response to the customer's request to compare against Tray.io; the sales lead used the pilot as the path to a purchase decision.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: I'll write them up and send them back so we're agreed rather than remembering differently.
evidence.context: Sales committed to scoping the evaluation with success criteria agreed in writing, including a build-by-customer-team test and time-logging, and to send the four criteria back. — Next-step and evaluation-structure approach for a new-business trial.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: And a perfectly valid outcome is "don't buy OrbitFlow" if the existing approach meets the criteria more cheaply.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow AE stated that not buying OrbitFlow is a valid outcome if the status quo meets criteria more cheaply, and proposed defining the pilot against status quo and alternatives. — Stated approach to the customer's goals in a new business evaluation; customer compared against Workato and improving existing tools.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: a valid outcome is
evidence.context: The AE said that a pilot should be measured against the status quo and Power Automate, and that 'don't buy' is a valid outcome. — Closing approach to the evaluation; openly allowed a no-purchase result.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: It might be. I'd rather you concluded that in July than in month five.
evidence.context: Vendor framed the competitive bar honestly as beating Zapier plus better documentation, not beating doing nothing, and said the prospect might conclude to stay put. — Competitive and objection framing for a new-business prospect.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: It's slow, but it's honest, and a slow honest timeline is worth more to me than a fast invented one.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow framed the timeline honestly rather than promising a fast close, citing past missed Q3 dates. — Vendor response to customer's slow procurement and architecture timeline (September review, Q4 procurement, early next year production).

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: A slow honest deal is worth more than a fast imaginary one.
evidence.context: The AE stated a preference for an honest, slower deal over a fast forecast, and accepted that no decision would happen this year. — Customer said realistically no decision this year, budgeting starts October; vendor accepted timing rather than pushing.

claims.text: Prospect-call candour took the form of honesty about competitors and price: Greenline was told Microsoft wins on pure per-seat cost, and Ember's vendor said it would rather lose to a documented decision. Written follow-ups replaced verbal commitments on compliance, for example the written UK residency answer for Harbor Legal.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: I'm not going to pretend we can beat bundled licensing on price. If the decision is purely cost per seat, Microsoft wins and everyone knows it.
evidence.context: On the Power Automate price objection, the AE conceded OrbitFlow cannot beat bundled licensing on price and reframed the case around operational cost. — Objection handling for an incumbent bundled-licence comparison.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: I'd rather we lose to a documented decision than lose to a two-month detour.
evidence.context: When the customer raised the 'keep scripts and document them' option, the vendor chose to address it openly in the pilot criteria rather than position Tray as the only alternative, and said it would rather lose to a documented decision than to a long internal detour. — Competitive and status-quo objection handling on a prospect call; the customer confirmed it would not satisfy the auditor.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: I won't dress a roadmap item as a capability.
evidence.context: The sales lead refused to present a roadmap item as an existing capability, and declined to answer a compliance question (UK data residency) on the call, committing instead to a written answer. — Customer asked for firm yes/no answers rather than roadmap promises; vendor separated confirmed capability from roadmap and deferred the answer to writing.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: I'll get you a definitive answer within the week.
evidence.context: The solutions engineer declined to answer the UK residency question on the call and committed to a definitive written answer within a week. — Customer pressed on UK residency, which may be a gate for public-sector clients; the vendor refused a verbal yes.

claims.text: Renewal candour was proactive disclosure of things the vendor might have kept quiet: overage waivers at Lumen, the AI consumption cost and the governance gap at Halberd, and the notice deadline at Pinewood.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: May was a judgement call. I'd rather tell you now than have it look like a discovery in the renewal.
evidence.context: Vendor proactively disclosed and waived overages rather than letting the customer discover them at renewal, and admitted one waiver was a judgement call. — Overage/billing handling in a renewal; the March waiver was for a Salesforce-side outage, the May one for proactive flagging.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: AI usage sits within your run allocation but there's a consumption element.
evidence.context: The AI feature has a consumption-based cost element on top of the run allocation, which the vendor said would be quantified in the renewal papers and was not expected to change the renewal. — Commercial add-on surfaced during the renewal, proactively flagged by the vendor so the customer would not be surprised.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: I'd rather point that out than have your own auditor point it out.
evidence.context: The vendor proactively raised a governance gap (no defined promotion or change control on production workflows) during the renewal, rather than waiting for the customer or an auditor to find it. — Account management concern raised unprompted in a renewal call; it is a risk to the customer rather than a sales upsell, and the customer reacted with surprise.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: I'm not going to auto-renew you into a twelve-month contract you didn't intend to sign.
evidence.context: The AE advised the customer to serve notice to stop the auto-renew, disclosing the 60-day notice deadline (30 September) that the customer did not know about, and said he would not auto-renew them into a 12-month contract they did not intend to sign. — Contract/term handling in renewal; vendor proactively disclosed a notice deadline that favours the customer's exit.
